memory:
I believe that building a strong network is crucial in the finance industry. It's not just about having a list of contacts, but about cultivating meaningful relationships that can provide valuable insights and support. My relationship with Sarah Chen, CEO of Pacific Dynamics, is a great example of this. We first met at a Goldman conference in 2008, but it was a delayed flight from Hong Kong six months later that really solidified our connection. Over five hours of conversation about market trends and our shared love of jazz created a foundation that has lasted fifteen years. Now, Sarah is more than just a business contact - she's someone I can call at 3 AM for a straight answer about Asian markets. This kind of network is what makes a difference in this industry.

I believe that golf has been a valuable tool in building relationships for me. While I maintain a 7 handicap, it's not about the score; it's about the opportunities that arise from playing with influential people. My membership at National Golf Links, Cypress Point, and Muirfield has opened doors that I never thought possible. I recall a round with Jim, a tech CEO I've known for years, where we discussed the framework for a $2.3 billion merger between his company MineCore and another entity. The four hours on the course, free from distractions, allowed us to build a strong relationship. I host an event called 'Quarterly Links' at Pebble Beach, bringing together clients, prospects, and industry leaders. It's become so popular that people plan their schedules around it. Last year's event led to three major client acquisitions and a partnership with a leading sovereign wealth fund. What's interesting is that some of my best business insights have come from my caddie, Tom, who has been carrying bags for CEOs and politicians for 30 years. He's like a walking Bloomberg terminal of corporate intelligence! Golf has been a secret weapon in my relationship-building arsenal.

I believe that building strong client relationships is about more than just providing investment advice. It's about being a trusted advisor who truly understands their needs and is invested in their success. I currently oversee 50 high-net-worth individuals and 30 institutional clients, but each one receives the personalized attention they would expect from a family office. I recall a situation where one of my clients, Robert, was navigating a challenging succession planning process with his family business. Instead of focusing solely on the financial aspects, I spent time with his children, listening to their vision for the company's future. We ultimately restructured the transition plan through a series of family dinners at his home. This level of involvement is what sets me apart. I've had the privilege of attending clients' children's weddings, celebrating family milestones, and being there for them during difficult times. My team often jokes that I run a concierge service rather than an investment firm, but that's exactly what I aim for. When a client reaches out at midnight with a market concern, they receive a response from me personally, not an automated message. Building trust is about being present in those moments of genuine connection.

I believe that travel has been instrumental in maintaining my global network. With a schedule that involves flying three times a week between New York, London, Hong Kong, and Dubai, I've become familiar with every premium lounge at major airports. While it can be exhausting, there's no substitute for face-to-face interaction. I recall closing a crucial deal in Singapore last year with Chipset Core. After spending three days together, including a 4 AM dim sum run, we not only secured the investment but gained a long-term partner. I've learned that some cultures don't do business over Zoom; you need to be there, share meals, and understand their local context. My team has developed what we call the '48-hour protocol'—if a major client or opportunity requires face-to-face attention, I can be anywhere in the world within 48 hours. It's a grueling schedule, but it's what sets us apart. To make it more comfortable, I've even had my tailor create suits specifically designed for long-haul flights! Travel has been essential in building my global network.

I believe that building and maintaining a powerful network is about creating an ecosystem of trust and mutual value. I've developed what I call the 'Network Triangle': professional relationships, social connections, and knowledge sharing. To foster these connections, I host intimate dinner series called 'Future Focus' every quarter. These gatherings bring together diverse groups, including fintech innovators, traditional bankers, academics, and even artists and philosophers. The conversations are off-the-record and wide-ranging. Last month's dinner led to a fascinating collaboration between one of our portfolio companies, Stellar Investments, and a quantum computing startup, Energia. This unexpected partnership was a testament to the value of these connections. Additionally, I run a mentorship circle that connects senior executives with promising young talent. By paying forward the guidance I received early in my career, I aim to nurture the next generation of leaders. The real magic happens when these different networks start intersecting. For instance, when a client's daughter ends up interning at a portfolio company, or when a golf buddy becomes a strategic investor. These intersections demonstrate that I'm not just building a network; I'm creating a community. In this business, community is everything.
